title: Indian-Origin Truck Driver Charged in Ohio Crash That Killed Woman, 50
excerpt: Manjit Singh, 39, of Fresno, California, faces an aggravated vehicular homicide charge after a September 2 head-on collision on US 68; ICE has lodged a detainer as DHS ties the case to federal immigration policy.
body:
• Manjit Singh, 39, of Fresno, California, has been charged with aggravated vehicular homicide after a September 2 head-on crash on US 68 in Brown County, Ohio, that killed Brenda Watson, 50.
  • Ohio State Highway Patrol investigators say Singh's 2019 Volvo tractor-trailer crossed into the southbound lane while attempting to pass another vehicle; a witness told investigators he was speeding and had ample time and space to merge back.
  • The Department of Homeland Security says Singh entered the US illegally through Arizona in October 2023, was later granted work authorization, and obtained a commercial driver's license from California; ICE has lodged a detainer with Brown County Jail.
  • DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin has tied the case to immigration enforcement and licensing policy, citing it as part of a pattern of fatal crashes involving non-citizen drivers holding California-issued licenses.

PLEASANT TOWNSHIP, Ohio — An Indian-origin semi-truck driver has been charged with aggravated vehicular homicide after a head-on crash on a rural Ohio highway killed a 50-year-old woman on September 2, and federal immigration authorities have lodged a detainer against him as the case becomes the latest flashpoint in a political fight over immigration enforcement and commercial driver's licensing.

Manjit Singh, 39, of Fresno, California, was driving a 2019 Volvo tractor-trailer northbound on US 68 near Hamer Road in Brown County's Pleasant Township around 9 p.m. when he attempted to pass another northbound vehicle and crossed into the southbound lane, striking a Chevrolet Cruze driven by Brenda Watson, 50, of West Union, according to the Ohio State Highway Patrol and court records. Watson died at the scene. Singh was not injured.

Context & Background

According to court records and police reports cited by local outlets, a witness told investigators that Singh was speeding and had "ample time and space" to merge back into the northbound lane before the collision. He was arrested after the crash and charged with aggravated vehicular homicide. The crash remains under investigation.

The Department of Homeland Security released a statement on September 9 laying out Singh's immigration history as described by federal authorities. According to DHS, Singh illegally entered the United States through Arizona in October 2023 and was encountered by US Border Patrol before being released into the country. DHS said he applied for work authorization in July 2024, which was granted in August 2024. The department also said Singh had obtained a commercial driver's license from California.

US Immigration and Customs Enforcement lodged a detainer with the Brown County Jail the day after Singh's arrest, asking jail officials to notify the agency before releasing him so he can be taken into federal custody and removed from the country, DHS said.

"He has no business being in our country or on our roads, but because of the reckless open borders of the Biden Administration and the sanctuary policies of Gavin Newsom's California, he was able to obtain a CDL that allowed him behind the wheel of a semi-truck."

— Markwayne Mullin, DHS Secretary

Impact & Analysis

DHS has framed the case as evidence of failures in immigration enforcement and state licensing policy. In its statement, the department cited several other cases involving non-citizens who it said held licenses issued in California and were later charged with crimes or involved in fatal crashes elsewhere: Rajinder Kumar of India, who DHS said jackknifed his semi-truck on an Oregon highway in November 2025, killing a newlywed couple; Harjinder Singh of India, who DHS said made an illegal U-turn in his semi-truck in St. Lucie County, Florida, in August 2025, killing three people; and Gunpreet Singh and Jasveer Singh of India, for whom ICE lodged detainers in January after they were arrested for smuggling more than 300 pounds of cocaine in a semi-truck in Putnam County, Indiana.

The department expressed condolences to Watson's family.

Diaspora Angle

The case lands amid a broader national debate over whether non-citizens, including undocumented immigrants and asylum seekers, should be eligible for commercial driver's licenses, and over the enforcement priorities of federal immigration agencies under the current administration. The rhetoric surrounding the case — including DHS's description of Singh — reflects how individual criminal cases are increasingly being used as policy arguments in the immigration debate. The charges against Singh are allegations; his criminal case is proceeding in Ohio, and the detainer means immigration enforcement proceedings will run in parallel.

What's Next

Singh remains held in the Brown County Jail under the ICE detainer. His criminal case will move through the Ohio courts, where he faces the aggravated vehicular homicide charge. Under the detainer, jail officials are asked to alert ICE before any release, at which point federal authorities could take him into custody for removal proceedings — meaning the immigration case may determine his future in the United States regardless of the criminal outcome.
nri_angle: A fatal Ohio crash involving an Indian-origin truck driver has become the latest flashpoint in the national debate over immigration enforcement and commercial driver's license rules.
author: Diaspora Desk
